Chapter 2: Recognizing the Subtle Habits That Undermine Progress
Once you realize it's time for a change, the next step is figuring out what, exactly, is holding you back. And here's the tricky part—it's usually not some big, obvious mistake. More often, it's those tiny, everyday habits that quietly pile up and get in the way of real progress. They're subtle, and sometimes even come from good intentions, so spotting them takes a bit of honest reflection.
Think about it like this: imagine walking with a pebble in your shoe. At first, it barely registers. But after a while? It starts to slow you down. In leadership and professional growth, these “pebbles” show up as habitual, almost automatic behaviors. They might’ve helped you once, but now they just create friction.
If you look closely, these habits usually fall into a few big categories. Maybe you recognize some of these:
There’s the urge to win every little debate, even when it doesn’t matter. Or the feeling that you always need to add your two cents to every conversation, whether it’s needed or not. Some folks can’t help but pass judgment, or offer advice nobody asked for. Others might forget to give credit where it’s due, or keep information to themselves—sometimes without even realizing it.
Then there’s the reflex to claim responsibility for someone else’s success, or the hesitation to admit when you’ve messed up. And let’s not forget making excuses or shifting blame instead of owning our actions.
On their own, each of these sounds pretty minor. But over time, together, they can really damage trust and teamwork. For instance, always needing to win can turn a friendly chat into a competition, making it hard for others to speak up. Constantly “adding value” might mean your team feels like their ideas never quite measure up—and that’s draining.
Picture a leader who, in every meeting, just has to tweak or top every suggestion. They may think they’re helping, but after a while, their teammates stop sharing ideas, convinced their input won’t matter. Morale and initiative start to fade away.
Withholding information is another habit that sneaks in. Maybe it feels easier to keep things close, or to avoid tough conversations. But without transparency, suspicion grows, and people stop sharing openly.
And when recognition is overlooked, even unintentionally, it stings. High achievers often assume good work speaks for itself, but without real acknowledgment, teammates can feel invisible and unappreciated.
Here’s something important: these habits don’t come from a place of malice or even incompetence. Most of the time, they’re just leftovers from past successes—behaviors that once set you apart, but now get in the way. The hardest part is that they’re almost invisible to us. They’re so ingrained, we barely notice them.
So, what can you do? The answer starts with self-awareness. That means taking time to reflect, and—maybe even more importantly—asking for honest feedback from others. It isn’t always comfortable. It might challenge how you see yourself. But it’s a crucial step if you want to grow and lead more effectively.
One practical way to uncover these habits is to ask trusted colleagues for their perspective. This doesn’t have to be formal—it could be a simple conversation, or part of a structured feedback process. What matters most is creating a space where people feel safe to be honest, and you’re truly open to hearing it.
So, the big takeaway from this chapter? The real second step in personal and professional growth is spotting those subtle habits that quietly hold you back. They might be rooted in good intentions, but they’re tough to see on your own. By shining a light on these behaviors—especially with help from others—you can finally start making the changes that matter most.
